source.title_on_document: Effects of Generative AI-Assisted Instruction on Creativity and Multidimensional Design Skills in Advertising Design Education: A Quasi-Experimental Study

supplement.holds: No supplementary material is mentioned. Data are 'not publicly available due to ethical and privacy restrictions' (PDF p. 16, printed p. 623, Data Availability).

paper_design_summary: Two intact second-year Digital Media classes at a college in China (85 students) took the same 8-week advertising design course from the same instructor. Class B (42 students) used Dreamina AI for concept generation, copywriting ideation, and visual exploration from Week 4 to Week 8; Class A (43 students) worked with traditional methods and no generative AI. Posters from Project 1 (pre-test, no AI for anyone) and Project 3 (post-test, AI available to the experimental class) were scored by three expert evaluators on a 100-point rubric with five dimensions (theme design, creativity, audience relevance, visual effects, copywriting), and post-test scores were compared by ANCOVA controlling for pre-test scores.

studies.label: Quasi-experiment, advertising design course (two intact classes)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Intact classes to GAI-assisted instruction (Class B) or traditional instruction (Class A)
assignment.quote: Due to constraints imposed by actual teaching arrangements, intact classes were used as experimental units without random assignment.

arms.name: GAI-assisted instruction (Class B, experimental)
arms.description: Instruction integrated with Dreamina AI from Week 4 to Week 8 for concept generation, copywriting ideation, and visual exploration; students had to refine AI outputs in design software, and unmodified AI images could not be submitted

arms.name: Traditional instruction (Class A, control)
arms.description: Same instructor, same projects and guidance; conventional design process (instructor guidance, brainstorming, hand-drawn sketching, digital production) without GAI tools

participants.exclusions: None stated. Tables 2 to 6 report N = 43 control and N = 42 experimental, matching the 85 participants in Section 3.1.
participants.who: Second-year college students majoring in Digital Media at the author's institution, aged 18 to 23, who had completed first-year design theory courses
participants.quote: This study was conducted at a college in China. The participants were 85 second-year college students majoring in Digital Media at the author's institution, aged 18 to 23.

ai_tool.name_model: Dreamina AI (generative AI platform for visual generation, concept exploration, and text-based ideation; no model version stated)
ai_tool.how_used: Experimental group used Dreamina AI during Project 2 (Weeks 4-5, practice) and Project 3 (Weeks 6-8, post-test) to generate design concepts, slogans, and visual elements, then refined the outputs in professional design software; the instructor demonstrated GAI use and gave guidance on prompt construction. Direct submission of unmodified AI-generated images was not permitted. (PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 614-615, Sections 3.2 and 3.3.3)

task.description: Advertising poster design projects. Pre-test: Project 1, Mid-Autumn Festival themed poster (Weeks 2-3, no AI for either group). Post-test: Project 3, public welfare poster on caring for empty-nest elderly (Weeks 6-8). Scored on a 100-point rubric: theme design 20, creativity 25, audience relevance 15, visual effects 20, copywriting 20.
task.duration: 8-week course (64 credit hours, 8 hours per week); intervention Weeks 4-8 (5 weeks); post-test project Weeks 6-8

outcomes.name: Creativity dimension of the post-test poster (Project 3)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric dimension 'creativity' (25 points max) assessing originality, novelty, and conceptual innovation; mean of three professional evaluators with more than ten years of experience; ICC for the five dimensions ranged 0.842 to 0.913 (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 616-617, Section 3.3.4). Main analysis is ANCOVA on post-test scores controlling for pre-test (Table 4). Robustness variants: raw pre/post means and mean differences in Table 5 (PDF p. 12, printed p. 619) and an independent-samples t-test on gain scores in Table 6 (PDF p. 13, printed p. 620): control gain 0.56 (SD 0.98, N 43) vs experimental gain 3.79 (SD 1.18, N 42), t = -13.71, df = 83, mean difference -3.23, p < 0.001.

contrasts.reported: ANCOVA adjusted means (controlling for pre-test): Experimental 21.79 (Std. Error 0.15, N = 42) vs Control 18.54 (Std. Error 0.15, N = 43); F = 191.85, p < 0.001, partial eta squared = 0.70. Raw post-test means (Table 5): Experimental 21.81 (SD 1.09) vs Control 18.53 (SD 1.20); pre-test 18.02 (SD 0.52) vs 17.98 (SD 0.64).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 619), Table 4 and Table 5; prose on PDF p. 11 (printed p. 618), Section 4.3

outcomes.name: Overall advertising design performance of the post-test poster (total rubric score)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total score (maximum 100) across the five rubric dimensions (theme design, creativity, audience relevance, visual effects, copywriting); mean of three expert evaluators; ICC for the total score 0.927 (PDF p. 10, printed p. 617). ANCOVA on post-test total controlling for pre-test total. The four non-creativity dimensions are also reported separately in Table 4 (PDF p. 12, printed p. 619): theme design F = 118.81, eta2 = 0.59; audience relevance F = 101.89, eta2 = 0.55; visual effects F = 115.97, eta2 = 0.59; copywriting F = 130.21, eta2 = 0.61; all p < 0.001.

contrasts.reported: Experimental group N = 42, Mean 86.81, SD 4.59, Adjusted mean 86.85, Std. error 0.70; Control group N = 43, Mean 74.65, SD 5.07, Adjusted mean 74.62, Std. error 0.69; F(1, 82) = 156.48, p < 0.001, partial eta squared = 0.66.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 fails: intact classes were used without random assignment (PDF p. 6, printed p. 613, Section 3.1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 614, Section 3.2). Criterion 2 is met with 85 students analyzed (42 experimental, 43 control; PDF p. 6, Section 3.1; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 618-619, Tables 3-4). Criterion 3 is met: three expert evaluators scored the student-produced posters on five dimensions, including creativity, and a total rubric score (PDF p. 9, printed p. 616, Section 3.3.4). AI remained available to the experimental class during production of the post-test poster (PDF p. 8, printed p. 615, Section 3.3.3). The four added quality/appropriateness outcomes also answer with_ai. Under the codebook, this nonrandomized comparison remains observational context and is not core-eligible.

one_line_finding: In two intact classes (42 with Dreamina AI, 43 without), the AI class scored higher on the creativity dimension of the post-test poster after controlling for pre-test (adjusted means 21.79 vs 18.54 out of 25, F = 191.85, p < 0.001, partial eta squared = 0.70; PDF p. 12, printed p. 619, Table 4) and on the total rubric score (adjusted means 86.85 vs 74.62 out of 100, F(1, 82) = 156.48, p < 0.001, partial eta squared = 0.66; PDF p. 11, printed p. 618, Table 3).
notes: The candidate record's venue field gives pp. 948-996; the PDF prints pp. 608-626. The record lists only Zhang as author; the document names Yaling Zhang and Lu Zhu (Assumption University, Thailand), with the study conducted at a college in China. Pre-test (Project 1) was produced without AI by both classes; the post-test (Project 3) was produced with Dreamina AI available to the experimental class only. The instructor and the three raters are not described as blind to condition. The ANCOVA treats students as independent although assignment was by class (two clusters).

Each records its rubric definition, Table 4 adjusted means and standard errors, N, F, p, and partial eta squared, and Table 5 raw means and standard deviations. Table 5 and Table 6 robustness variants are identified in measure_detail.
